title: Mary across the churches
hookLine: churches call Mary God-bearer; Catholics and Orthodox honor her highly; Protestants honor her as a model disciple

cards: A young woman hurries into the hill country of Judea to see her cousin Elizabeth. Her name is Mary, and she is carrying news she can hardly explain.
She barely gets through the door before Elizabeth, old and herself unexpectedly pregnant, cries out: "And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" The mother of my Lord.
Christians have thought hard about that phrase, and one Greek title stands behind much of it.

teach.b: Theotokos is Greek for God-bearer: the one who gave birth to God. That sounds bold, and it's meant to.
But the title is really about her son. If the child she carried is one person, truly God and truly human, then the woman who bore him bore God.
When this was argued in the early church, a council at Ephesus defended the title, and Orthodox and Catholic prayer still uses it. From there the churches honor her in different ways.

Orthodox Christians sing hymns to the Theotokos and keep her icons close. Catholics pray the Hail Mary and the rosary, and teach that she was conceived without sin and taken up body and soul into heaven.

Protestant churches generally don't pray to her, and don't hold those last teachings as doctrine. They honor her as the model disciple, who heard God's word and said, "be it unto me according to thy word."
At a wedding in Cana, when the wine ran out, she told the servants: "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it." She points away from herself, to him.
Then there's her own song in Luke, the Magnificat: "My soul doth magnify the Lord, and my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour."

teach.h: ALL GENERATIONS SHALL CALL ME BLESSED.
teach.b: And a few lines later, the line behind today's carry: "from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed." A young woman from Nazareth says that about herself, and it's in every church's Bible.
The churches argue over how to honor her. None of them disputes that she is blessed.

how: Catholics pray the Hail Mary and the rosary; Orthodox Christians sing hymns to the Theotokos in their services; Protestant churches read Mary's song, the Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55), and honor her as a model of faith, especially around Christmas.

games.q: you're at a wedding in Cana. the wine has run out. Mary turns to the servants. what does she say?
o: "whatsoever he saith unto you, do it."
"tell the guests the feast is over."
games.why: she points them to her son. then he turns water into wine. it's one reason Protestants honor her as the model disciple: she sends attention to him.

practice: Open Luke chapter one at verse forty-six, Mary's song, in any Bible or on your phone, and read it slowly, once, noticing who goes up and who comes down: the proud scattered, the mighty put down from their seats, the lowly lifted, the hungry filled.
Then sit with whichever line stays. If you pray, let her words rise as your own for a moment; if you don't, just let the song be heard.

wordCard.voice: Theotokos. Greek for God-bearer: Mary, the mother of the child Christians call truly God and truly human.
